utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm sorry to have kept the Court waiting; I'm sorry that Mr. Kljuic has been kept waiting in particular. But we have been trying to arrive at a Court sitting schedule for the week of the 8th of November. We shall sit on the morning of the 8th of November, but difficulties occurred about the afternoon, and there's an unavailability at the moment of courtroom space. We shall sit in the afternoon of the 9th and 10th; no sitting on the 11th; and we shall sit on the morning of the 12th. Now, that is the current schedule. I wish I could say it's final, but I can't, because I'm not sure about the courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If possible, we will sit on the afternoon of the 8th. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The position so far as Mr. Kljuic is concerned is that I had all but concluded my examination-in-chief on the last occasion; I reserved the possibility of asking a few further questions. Since then, the minutes of the meeting of the 27th of December, Exhibit 2717, have been translated into 2717A, into English, and I'm not sure of the state of translation into French at the moment. There are two questions I intend to ask the witness about that version now it's been properly translated, and there are a couple of other documents that ought to be produced by the witness that have come available to us since he gave his evidence on the first occasion, and with your leave, I'll just deal with those matters now and move on with one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I should add this, that today, because of other engagements, it's necessary that we adjourn sometime before the usual luncheon adjournment, towards quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While we're dealing with administrative matters, can I apologise now for my absence at half past 2.00; I have to attend on the other Chamber in relation to a matter that may or may not take some time. Ms. Somas will, of course, be dealing with matters in my absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, can I first ask you, please, to look at Exhibit Z1,1 and Z1,1A, which I hope are before the Chamber, or will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These were distributed to the Defence yesterday, in fact. This is a tidying-up operation, although it's a document that may become significant, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The document I'm asking you to look at, Mr. Kljuic, in the original form, is that the Statute of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina itself, as opposed to the Croatian statute, which may be the only statute we had available on the last occasion?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: [In English] May I speak, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will say to you it was -- the Statute of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina was slightly modified, and that was one of the chief bones of contention between the Bosnian Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina and those who believed that the Bosnian-Herzegovinian HDZ should be a subsidiary of the Croatian HDZ. Namely, in the beginning, there was a lot of argument going on as to what our party in Bosnia-Herzegovina should be called. Evidently the democratisation in the former Yugoslavia, which started first in Slovenia and Croatia, in Bosnia it was meeting with a number of difficulties, and it was quite naturally that the Croat people were first organised in Zagreb through the HDZ, and we transposed it to Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I refused it to be called HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and with the group which supported me, we succeeded to call it the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is an identical name for the party in both federal units. In the west, of course, it is not a problem, because you have very many conservative parties in various countries of west or northern Europe, where you have Democratic Christians, so on and so forth, so we are one and the same people. We share the concept, but I nevertheless thought that Bosnia and Herzegovina should have its own party. And furthermore, we also modified the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to cut you short if there is something material to say, but I think you have given a very full explanation of the derivation of the Statute, and I'm going to pass on subject to just one detail matter. If you would look at Article 33, page 7, in the English, and it's on page 6 in the original. Was the Statute -- did the Statute ordain that there should in the presidency be a president and one vice-president? In the event, there may have been two vice-presidents, but the Statute allowed for one; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Is it true that there were two vice-presidents? You must realise that in the situation as there was, these statutes were drafted under the Communist authorities. They would not allow us to register, to become politically active, so that we had to do these things very hastily so as to contribute towards the legitimisation of our parties. However, after the convention of the 23rd and 24th of March '91 in Mostar, the Statute was then gone through and clarified, and then it became clear that there were two vice-presidents. We always had to emphasise the first vice-president and the second vice-president. The first vice-president, unfortunately, Vitomir Lukic, I have to say one of the greatest brains in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a writer, a university professor, died in late '91, as the Minister for Religious Affairs in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and after that there were no more conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other two documents associated with formalities may be documents you can't help us with. They are available. One is 4139,1 and 4139,1A, and the other one is 1473,1. Were you aware of when the High Court in Sarajevo was notified of the change of president from yourself to Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I don't know when the Court was notified, but it is not true that Dario Kordic succeeded me as President. Please, let me tell you. I submitted my resignation on the 2nd of February, '92. Under the Statute I continued as President, that is the outgoing President, because that was what the Statute said, which we had taken over from Croatia. And I protected of course my position, just as President Tudjman did in Croatia. So the solution for this problem was to hold a convention. Because under the Statute only a convention can dismiss a President, of course. They were not happy about the convention because my departure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These matters can all be gone into. Your Honour, so far as these documents are concerned, they are Court documents. So probably they are documents that can effectively produce themselves.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I don't know that it was ever registered in a Sarajevo Court, perhaps in a Court in Mostar that Kordic's appointment, Kordic's election was registered. Without me, they had to modify Statute, they brought Professor Brkic, and then some War Presidency brought Mate Boban --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What I was going to say, the documents effectively prove themselves. They can be commented on by other witnesses later and dealt with in argument. If there is any objection to their being produced, they can be produced by another witness. But it would seem to me they are best dealt with now, probably. I see Mr. Naumovski wants to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. All I wanted to say was that this document is outside the time frame of the indictment and is quite irrelevant. The material is of 1996 and it is quite irrelevant. It does not apply to Mr. Kordic's case. Besides, it's not signed, the original seal or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think the simplest matter is for it to be produced. We will decide what weight, if any, to give to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The two documents are, and I am not going to trouble the witness with them further, 1439,1 and 1A and 1473,1 and 1A. And with their production I move on swiftly to the two remaining topics which I want to deal with very shortly with this witness. The first topic is a couple of passages from the document now translated, which is 2717A, for those following in English. And I have, I think, the appropriate references in the original document 2717 for the witness himself to follow. The first passage is at page 10 of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could it be placed on the ELMO, please, because the interpreters don't have their copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry that the interpreters don't have it. It's remiss of me not to have checked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 10 in there. And in the original for Mr. Kljuic to follow, I think it's 4/5. Page 4/5. This is one of two passages I am going to read. Then ask for your comments, Mr. Kljuic. Mr. Boban at the meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, could you please remind us which document is it? We do have the number, but what is this document, apart from the number? We have it on the ELMO. I simply wish to know what kind of a document is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will recall that there was a meeting on the 27th of December, 1991 attended by, amongst others, the President of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Tudjman, and other officials, including this witness; that the meeting was minuted, probably tape-recorded and transcribed; that the transcription was provided to the witness at an early stage and shortly after the meeting itself. On the last occasion we went through several passages of the transcribed minutes or notes or recording of the meeting, but we didn't have any other translations, official or otherwise, apart from partial translation available. And so what we are looking at now is the official translation by the Tribunal of that original transcript in B/C/S or Croatian of the meeting. And the two passages I am going to ask the witness to deal with both relate to what was being said by Mr. Boban, and at page 10. And I'll turn to the French. And if I go too fast then I'll be corrected, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Boban say as follows: "All of you know that recently, there has been an alternative entity in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather a continuity of the policies of the Croatian Democratic Union and the Croatian people in general. Something new exists called the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosnia and the Croatian community of Posavina in the north of Bosnia. This idea was embraced, in this sense, as a framework for the expression of the political will of the Croatian people whose most prominent mouthpiece is the Croatian Democratic Union. The people have placed their full trust in the leadership, setting up Croatian communities which represent political, cultural and economic attributes of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Should Bosnia and Herzegovina remain an independent state without any ties with the former disintegrating or any future, Yugoslavia, or should Bosnia itself disintegrate, the area where about 650.000 Croats live would implement internationally recognised democratic methods proclaiming this to be independent Croatian territory, which will accede to the State of Croatia, but only at such a time as the Croatian leadership, in whom our people until now have placed their complete trust, should decide that the moment and time had come." The second passage in the English can be found at page 21, and in the original at pages 8/2 and 8/3. And Mr. Boban said on page 21 in the English: "The founding municipalities of the HZHB/Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna/now have a population, which according to the census is 55% Croatian, 27% Muslim and 9% Serbian and the rest are none of the above. "However, because municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina were created, similarly as in Croatia, by composing Serbian and Muslim population in the territory of Croatia or vice versa, by cleansing border areas, practically border areas of Herceg-Bosnia, this creates approximately 65% of the Croatian population in Herceg-Bosnia." Then he says: "And, pardon me, the most recent data are 63%". So, Mr. Kljuic, in relation to the first passage where the linkage of territory to Croatia itself was referred to, was that something with which you agreed or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: It is completely irrelevant, if I agreed with it personally or not. What does matter is that such a Proclamation was completely contrary to the political platform of the HDZ adopted at a Mostar convention and before the elections, because, at the end of the story, were the elections on the basis of two political theses: The first, Bosnia-Herzegovina, a sovereign state equal -- on equal footing with all the other federal units; secondly, quality of the Croat people within Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that, after all, was our first and foremost political goal. Any other modification of the political platform, the political process, was to be reflected at a convention which should have taken place. But you must know that the situation in the former Yugoslavia was rapidly changing. Many people did not believe that Bosnia-Herzegovina would survive as a state. Even though it tried to explain those in Zagreb and to those in Sarajevo that -- on the Helsinki conference of 1974 it would have to remain one state. And after all, it was binding on both Croatian and subsequently Bosnia-Herzegovina because, having gained their independence, they also had to accede to a number of international treaties signed by the former Yugoslavia, so that it was directly violating the political platform. And those who are listening to it had to hear that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. If you would confine your answers, please, we will get on more quickly. We'll try and finish your evidence as soon as we can. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in relation to the second passage, Mr. Kljuic, the cleansing of border areas, was that, in your judgment, any proper function of the body that you had been instrumental in establishing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, but this is subject -- this subject was already covered by the Prosecutor during the examination-in-chief in July. Mr. Kljuic already answered this question. This is the continuation of the examination-in-chief. That is how I understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution is allowed to continue his examination. No doubt, he will do so quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kljuic, will you answer the question, and let it be very brief. Was this cleansing of border areas, was this part of the function of the body you had helped create, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: It was not part of the political programme, but, yes, that is what happened on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have only two other questions, at most, and they are these: The meeting at Siroki Brijeg on the 2nd of February, 1992, of which you've already spoken, was called by somebody called Drago Krpina. He was, I think, an official of the Croatia HDZ. Can you explain how such a person came to call a meeting of this type and for the purpose that we've heard about?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: When hard times began in Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the first road blocks and first protests erupted, the -- part of western Herzegovina did not have frequent contact with Sarajevo. Secondly, they did not recognise Sarajevo leadership as the leadership of the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina. They considered themselves members of an integral HDZ and recognised only the leadership in Zagreb. It took me a long time to discuss this problem with Mr. Tudjman, explaining to him that we had to teach them all that their central headquarters, central office was in Sarajevo, and that Sarajevo and Zagreb should hold normal consultation. But, as it was for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a document which was of crucial significant import for Bosnia-Herzegovina and for Croatia, unfortunately, part of the leadership which opposed me was not for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. Namely, you need to know, and it has been proven by now that there was a meeting in Karadjordjevo in Mr. Sarimic's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've covered this. The question is how this person from Croatia was able to call the meeting. And I think you've probably covered that. I am not going to ask any more questions and --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't answer your question. Excuse me. They were trying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If he wants to ask anything else, Mr. Kljuic, he will do so. Now, would you please let him be the judge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, because of these technical arrangements. Mr. Kljuic, may I introduce myself. My name is Naumovski, an attorney from Zagreb. I represent Mr. Dario Kordic. I have a series of questions for you and be kind enough to answer them. I have to ask you to make breaks in between my question and your answers so that what we are saying can be interpreted properly. So as to be as expeditious as possible, if you can please answer with a yes or a no, because that will speed things up. Mr. Kljuic, will you please tell us how many times have you spoken to the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I don't know who the investigators were, but I spoke three times two years ago, and then after that at the beginning of this year and before I came, before I entered the courtroom once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, were notes taken of those interviews? Was your statement written down? Was a record made?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: At first they took notes and I spoke. And then I made a statement in chronological order to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So there is a written report on what you told the investigators?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: There is a written record of what I signed as my official statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because the Defence has not received any statement of yours, and that is why this question was of importance to us. Do you have a copy on you, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No, I don't, but I can fax it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, apart from these interviews with the investigators, did you make a statement for the Commission for the Investigation of War Crimes attached to the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: That commission was formed on the 24th of April, 1992, and it was an excellent body. However, they had me replaced, so as to be able to manipulate that commission, and therefore I never made a statement for that commission for the collection of evidence of war crimes attached to the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We know, Mr. Kljuic, that you were a member and president of that commission. But then you mentioned manipulation. Who wanted to manipulate with the commission?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Well, I was replaced, and I heard on the radio one day. A thesis appeared in the newspapers that I would be a Bosnian Wiesenthal, but I must say that I cooperated very well and collected a great deal of documentation, and they had me replaced. Had they not done that, probably the list of people who would go to The Hague would have been quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but could you give us a name? Do you know who was the one who manipulated?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I don't know who it was. I just heard on the radio that I had been replaced and someone else had been chosen in my place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Will you please pay attention, because the interpreter is having difficulty in following you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You see, I was the first to make a mistake with regard to the speed. Tell me, please, this commission, while you were a member of it, did it conduct an investigation against Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No. I was replaced in 1994. Until then, as far as I know, there was no investigation, the more so as I was the political head, whereas legal experts were engaged; there were many young people among them, so that I didn't interfere with their work, but as far as I know, there was no such investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: A final question in the introduction: Knowing your political activities, is it correct to say that you did not wish to testify in court in closed session?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Why would I testify confidentially when that is my credo? My testimony could have all kind of repercussions if it were in closed session. It could encourage all kind of guesswork as to what I had said or not said. I felt it a moral obligation to say in public whatever I had to say. Even under communism, I acted in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us now go on, Mr. Kljuic, to the topic that you have been testifying about in the examination-in-chief, and that is the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina. Speaking about the Statute, you mentioned, but I think it is worth repeating, when the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina was founded in August 1990, Yugoslavia still existed?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So, essentially, those were the very first days of a multiparty system, and that is precisely why this Statute which has been produced in court today had to be in conformity with the regulations in force at the time of the former socialist Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, 1990, two or three months prior to the HDZ, the Party of Democratic Action was founded in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The Party of Democratic Action had its branches in Croatia, in Sandzak, in Macedonia, America, Germany, and various other places, didn't it? In Kosovo too?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And the fact that we have underlined the existence of the former common state, there were no formal or legal obstacles to the formation of parties which would act throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So by way of conclusion, when you became president of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Yugoslavia was still a viable state?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You mentioned that at one of the first meetings after you became president of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you defined the HDZ -- and let me quote you -- as a party advocating the interests of the Croatian people throughout. At the same meeting, and it was a meeting of the presidency, the executive board, and members of the municipal board of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, held on the 8th of October, 1990, and also attended by Mr. Gojko Susak, who was then Minister for Emigration in the Republic of Croatia, he stressed at the time -- and let me quote him -- that the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina should be led by you independently, and "as far as we are concerned, we can provide advice." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I beg your pardon for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have prepared a copy of the documents that we intend to use in the course of the cross-examination of Mr. Kljuic, so I'm not quite sure whether these documents have been distributed, so I should like to ask the registrar to do so, if it hasn't been done, for the witness, so that the witness can keep track of what we are saying. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, we've prepared this set of documents for you so that we shouldn't waste any time asking the registrar to provide them one by one. This is a document, Z21719 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you go there, Mr. Naumovski, have we got copies of these documents? Are they the Prosecution exhibits, or are they something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) They are all -- more than 90 per cent of Prosecution exhibits, with a "Z" letter, and we will be producing only a few new documents, of which we shall provide copies for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let us continue. The HDZ, as a party, also had its branch offices throughout the world, didn't it? In Germany, Sweden, the United States, and so on?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So please speak clearly for the record. As president of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you travelled abroad a lot, and you went to Zagreb frequently. As president of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you have contacts with President Tudjman and the other leaders of the HDZ in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you insisted on coordination and synchronisation of the work of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina and other HDZ organisations, especially the HDZ in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: As can be seen from document Z21712, which is the programme of work of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated from 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All this because you felt, I assume, that this was natural and necessary for the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to link up with Croats in other states, including the Croats in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But despite this coordination of activities, it was your opinion, as you said today in answer to a question from the Prosecution, that the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina was an independent party?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: That was what I struggled to achieve, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps this is the moment, Your Honours, for us to tender a document, an interview with Mr. Kljuic to a newspaper, Novi List, from Rijeka, on the 13th of October, 1991. We have the original and also a translation of that article into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I think you have a copy.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I don't need it. I know very well what I said. I'm ready to answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But just in case you need to consult the article --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No, no, I don't need it. Just give me the floor, and I will tell you whatever you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But let's wait for this to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, in that interview, you said, and I quote: "Regarding the HDZ in Zagreb and the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, relations are quite clear. The things that are of global significance, that are common for the whole Croatian people, that is our common concern, and we have quite identical positions. However, when it comes to concrete policies in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had complete autonomy, and nobody interfered nor exerted any influence." That is the gist of what we were talking about a moment ago, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that is how things were until the 2nd of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is what I was going to say. We are talking about the period while you were president of the HDZ; that is the main topic of our discussion.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you considered yourself independent, didn't you, as an individual?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: That was my principle in life, but it is not just a question of personal will. But you didn't mention something that is very important for an understanding of the situation. I explained last time why I had to recognise Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We will come to that.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I recognised Herceg-Bosna for them, and they recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina. Because if Bosnia-Herzegovina prevailed, then Herceg-Bosna could not prevail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We'll come to that topic later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I apologise to Your Honours. In the English translation, that is page 5, the last paragraph, the passage that I just read, and I apologise to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, can we go on now to another topic, which we could call the organisation of self-defence. A few chronological points for everyone to be able to follow. Already in 1990, the Serbs started to organise communities of municipalities and later on formed autonomous provinces of Krajina in Croatia, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And then the same thing, more or less, happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina became particularly worried after the so-called "SAO Krajina" on the 2nd of April, 1991 -- I'm talking about the Krajina in the Republic of Croatia -- proclaimed its secession from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Those were actually the beginnings of the disintegration of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I think one could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Their Honours have already had occasion to hear that tensions increased, and in the summer of 1991, the war actually started in the Republic of Croatia, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: At that time, both the JNA and the army of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina used the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a kind of training ground for the war against the Republic of Croatia, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Not only Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is a topic I had a great deal of problems over in Croatia. They said, "You're allowing our territory to be shot at from your territory," and I said to Susak, "But they are shooting from Mirkovci." Mirkovci is a well-known Chetnik village near Osijek. So this is something we could not prevent. And they used Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially after Slovenia broke off and after the barracks in Croatia were abandoned and where troops were pulled out from, so many troops focused in Bosnia. I witnessed the army's withdrawal from the Borongaj barracks. When people were drinking champagne, I was the only one who wasn't drinking. And when Mr. Tudjman asked me, "What is it? Aren't you happy that we've let them go from Borongaj?" I said, "Of course I'm not happy, because now they're going to come to Bosnia." So the fact is that the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was used for offensive operations against Croatia, that Serb elements from Bosnia-Herzegovina directly fired at Croatia, and this applies to the area of Posavina. But that reflected the balance of forces, because they also shot from the territory of Croatia against the defensive forces of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm trying to follow the record so that no error can creep in, but let us continue along those lines. As you said, the JNA, as it withdrew to Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the same time people were being mobilised in Bosnia-Herzegovina for the war in Croatia. This was a mobilisation of Croats and Muslims who were expected to join the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: You see, the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not allow that, and we prohibited the mobilisation of Croats and Muslims. But the Serb members of the presidency would not take part in that decision. They were Koljevic and Biljana Plavsic. So the Serbs voluntarily joined that army, and I believe that was the first time we gave the JNA a "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We'll come back to that a little later, but this is simply a chronological overview of the events which led up to everything that followed. So apart from this mobilisation and the withdrawal of JNA from Slovenia and Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina, what occurred was what was known as the tacit occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For instance, in June 1991, about 200 tanks arrived at Kupres, and Kupres, to remind Their Honours, is a strategic, very important plateau dividing Central Bosnia from western Herzegovina, you will agree, Mr. Kljuic; and then, again, in September '91, JNA reservists from Serbia and Montenegro came to Bosnia-Herzegovina to the surroundings of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel to speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you were among the first politicians in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is something you referred to in the interview with the Novi List of Rijeka, who warned of a plan according to which the Serbs, with the help of the JNA, wanted to gain control of the territory, not only of the Republic of Croatia but of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: You see, they are denying that now. It is true that I was the first to discover the project Ram, R-a-m. According to a conversation between Karadzic and Milosevic, they wanted to create a state up to Karolvac, Karlobag, and Virovitica, that would be its eastern border of this new state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: At the time, when these things were happening, the central authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina had still not undertaken anything to organise the defence of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina from aggression which was about to occur?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you. You have to know that the Communists handed over the weapons of the Territorial Defence to the army of Yugoslavia. Let us make it quite clear. Josip Broz knew very well what would happen after his death, and he created two parallel structures of armaments in the former Yugoslavia. One was the official army, the armed forces, and the other was a kind of Territorial Defence as in William Tell. However, when the Berlin wall came down, when the process of democratisation started in eastern Europe, all Communist politicians, with the exception of the Slovenes, allowed the weapons of the national defence to be transferred to the barracks of the Yugoslav army. These were vast amounts of money because the people had paid for those weapons and that is how the Communists allowed Milosevic via the army to gain such a dominant position in the former Yugoslavia. The presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for its part, was aware of its impotence, and the only thing it could do was to mobilise the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But that was in September, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that was all we could do, because the police were still armed and knew how to handle arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But let me interrupt you. When I said this, I had in mind the absence of official reactions to what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and by way of an example, the events in Ravno and so on. That is what I had in mind when I said that nothing was done in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I do not agree with you. I was disturbed by Ravno in particular, and we formed a commission of the government and the presidency to make an on-site inspection, and in the media we did a great deal to protect Ravno. But no one else did. We didn't have the strength to oppose the army. And the International Community remained passive. And this was the first massacre in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the other hand, we were not all unanimous in the presidency, I must tell you, because the Serb part of the presidency was very gloated at the time over this because it had demonstrated the strength of the Yugoslav People's Army, whereas some other people said that this wasn't their war. However, the impression --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I must ask you to stop now. The purpose of the examination is for questions and answers to be given. We will get on more quickly if we can deal with the matter crisply. Now, I think we've exhausted this topic, Mr. Naumovski. Could you move on to something else, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one single sentence, please. Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've said we've exhausted the topic. Would you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I should say that after this counsel has examined, Prosecution counsel will have the chance to re-examine. And if there are any relevant matters which he thinks should be taken up, he will do so. So you will have the opportunity to deal with anything else relevant. Now, let's move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let us continue this chronology, so-to-speak, by dealing with the subject which we might call the preparations of Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina for a defence. As document Z2731 shows, on the 4th of April, 1991, at the meeting of the presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a decision was reached to introduce duty shifts around the clock in the municipal committees of the HDZ throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Another document introduced a few days later at the session of the presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on the 16th of April 1991, and that is document Z2733, a higher degree of alert was introduced during these duty shifts, and all of this also took place in the Republic of Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Everything that we spoke about a few minutes ago, unequivocally, shows to the members of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially the presidency, that soon a war would break out in the Republic of Croatia, and that is why a series of measures was introduced in the bodies of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We touched upon the subject a few minutes ago. And perhaps we could put just two questions in this regard. In document Z2735, and that is the meeting held on the 10th of July 1991, that is to say the session of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the illegal mobilisation of the population is pointed out. That's what we mentioned a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And then in document Z2710 the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina is asked to stop sending young men into the army?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That they should do their military service in Bosnia-Herzegovina, et cetera, et cetera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And, finally, when a state of war was declared in the Republic of Croatia, you give a recommendation, and that is Z2744, and a special statement related to this, Z2743. You give this recommendation on the 26th of August, 1991 to Croats, not to send their children to the JNA any longer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, when you testified in July, page 5.253 to 5.254, you said, Mr. Kljuic, that you personally intervened after the first elections that were held in 1990, that Mr. Dario Kordic got a job as secretary of national defence, as it was then called, in the municipality of Busovaca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Although he did not meet the requirements, he did not have two years of experience, I ordered at the time that he be appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I assume that at that time you thought that he could help in the protection of Croats and Muslims; that is to say, that they should not be sent to do their military service. This is the subject that gained in prominence afterwards; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I said that since there were no Serbs in that municipality, that as many children of ours as possible should be sent to do their military service in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then after that in Croatia and Slovenia. This was our strategic interest, and it was only natural, because if they were to be sent to Serbia and Macedonia, then what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, in connection with this, you said in an interview that basically in August 1991 you prevented mobilisation of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you prevented some 300.000 people wearing JNA uniforms and simply trampling over Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Well, there is an objective I cannot discuss right now, you see, but my role was not to allow the project Ram to be carried out. The Yugoslav People's Army at that time had officers, weapons and they needed Muslims and Croats, and soldiers. And I think that they would have achieved their objective of reaching Karlobag very quickly, but then I issued an order that Croats do not leave, and I also made a great effort to convince not the leadership, but the people, the Muslim people, not to go. Because that was their war, just as it was ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And my last question in this respect. In view of the recommendation that you gave for Mr. Kordic, and in view of what we know that he did, and we imagine that you know too, do we agree that Mr. Kordic also, within the framework of his possibilities, and within his municipality, also assisted this effort; that is, that young Croatian and Muslim men do not go to the JNA and do not fight for the objectives of the already former JNA. I could call it that, I think?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Well, except for a few incidents that are negligible as far as this trial is concerned, during peacetime I had no objections to him. He was politically immature. He listened to Boban. But that can be tolerated. But as for his work in the municipality, I think that what he did, he did fairly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. We talked about Bosnia-Herzegovina a few minutes ago, about the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a training ground for attacks on the Republic of Croatia. Let us just mention some documents here now, for example, Z18. And, Mr. Kljuic, in July 1991 you said on television that the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if necessary, will defend the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first time that someone opposed the Yugoslav People's Army in that way. That was a statement that I made, and I said if the Republic of Croatia is attacked, that the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina would defend it. We did defend it. And I have to tell you one more thing. With gratitude, that about 10.000 Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina took part in the defence of Croatia. Later, they drew on that experience in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and many of them had Croat nicknames, like Zenga, Zagi, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is what I wish to infer right now, but since you said it, there is no need for me to repeat it. In addition to Croat young men, Muslim young men also went to wage war on Croatia, to defend it. Just one more thing. The statement that you made on television was basically supported by the conclusion of the presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the 31st of July 1991, and that is document Z736. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, there were a lot of statements of support, but this was quite a normal reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let us proceed. As we follow along parallel lines, what is going on in Croatia, I am now talking about the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 26th of August 1991, and that is document Z2744. You actually introduced extraordinary measures within the HDZ, didn't you, because of the war in Croatia? A kind of emergency?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If you agree, we could explain to the honourable judges how the preparations took place in terms of the military organisation of the HDZ, because you and the HDZ knew what would inevitably follow. So let us skip over the things that the honourable judges already know, and that is in June 1991 there was a war in the Republic of Slovenia. We already said what kind of actions were taken by the Serb paramilitary units in Croatia, that the war had already started. At that time, that is to say on the 10th of June 1991, and this is important in terms of our chronology, the Muslims established what they called the Muslim Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point we would like to tender a document. This is a document of the SDA party which confirms what I just said. So could we ask Mr. Kljuic to take a look at this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Copies for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D96/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could you please place the English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Well, now that I read who said it -- who signed it, I think I can say that it is authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Honourable Court who Mr. Hasan Cengic was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: At that time he did not hold a post within the government. He was in the party, but during the war he was the chief logistics man of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and after the war he held numerous offices before the OSC replaced him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Now that we are talking about this document. This was the first organisation of its kind in Bosnia-Herzegovina, wasn't it, in June 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I have to tell you that the situation on the ground was quite confused, that people were spontaneously getting armed. So it is quite unimportant when a party or a group of people found an official way of doing this. But I think, after the Serbs who got weapons from the JNA, all normal people tried to arm themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: There is no denying that, Mr. Kljuic, but I just wanted to mention something that you actually answered at the very beginning. Actually, I wanted to ask you or, rather, to have you confirm that at that time the party that had very good relations with the SDA -- I mean, you were not invited when this National Defence Council was established.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Well, you see, they were not invited when we Croats did the same thing. So it was something secret. However, until the present day I have not heard of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let us proceed. As for the chronology, I touched upon this because this took place a month before the HDZ, in addition to all other councils through which it tried to improve the situation on the ground, established a Security Council. That is document Z2735, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Well, it's not quite clear what the Security Council was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This was not for purposes of armament.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I didn't say that. No, no, no. This is coordination of all documents, and of the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I am not supposed to interject while you are speaking because then we have a problem with the transcript. You headed that Security Council, that is what the presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina decided; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And now what you said a few minutes ago, what you started telling me, the Security Council was basically established in order to bring an information together and also to coordinate work related to the security of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I just have to mention, by the way, for the sake of the transcript, that this decision of the 10th of July 1991 was confirmed in document Z10, less than a month later. However, Mr. Kljuic, Z16 is a very interesting document, and that is a conclusion of the Security Council that we were discussing just now, dated the 18th of September 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, I am going to stop you now. You are making speeches to the witness. Could you confine yourself, please, to asking him questions. You can make your points to us in due course, that you want to make about the documents. Now, as far as the witness is concerned, let us get on with his examination and confine yourself, if you would, to asking him questions. As I say, in due course you will make submissions to us and you can say what you want about the documents, but we'll get on more quickly if you simply ask the witness briefly about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will, Your Honour. Thank you. However, we agreed on most subjects and I simply wanted to speed up the answers. However, if the Honourable Trial Chamber views things differently, then I shall act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kljuic, very briefly, on the 18th of September 1991 the Security Council grew into the crisis staff. This was a higher level of organisation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: This was just a formal change in name. The situation in Croatia was getting ever more complicated, so we wanted to receive as much information as possible and to know how to take a position of our own. And, you know, this was quite a fashionable thing at the time. Everybody had crisis staffs at the time, so we had a crisis staff too. However, the purpose was not different at all .

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You were President of this crisis staff, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Who was your deputy? Mr. Boban, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it was, according to the very formation. He was vice-president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In this document, Z16, what is important is that in addition to this change of name into crisis staff, that is, essentially a decision was passed to establish organs related to structure and command. Remember, that's what you called it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This organ related to structure and command, what was its function?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I must tell you that at that time the war in Croatia was already very intensive. We Croats did not have many officers. And through this organisation we tried to take over officers from the JNA who were not compromised, and to take people who could help us in the defence of Croatia and possibly in the war in Bosnia that would follow. So politicians and party officials were not people that I could count on in terms of these activities, because they were amateur. I was an amateur too, although in the former Yugoslavia I held the name of captain. This was an initiative to bring together as many professional people as possible in order to assist the defence of Croatia and, if need be, in the future, of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can we agree, then, Mr. Kljuic, along the lines of what you said just now, that basically in this way a future body was being established; that is to say some kind of command of the future army? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that did not happen. My intention was to engage professional officers, however, those who were implementing this retained for themselves the right to command. And that is going to be the tragedy of the Croat people during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Very briefly, in relation to this subject. Document Z18 shows or, rather, on the basis of Z18 I would like to put a few questions. You started organising a network of these crisis staffs and structure and command -- professional commander organizations in the municipalities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you also started making lists of volunteers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Then you were also making records of personnel, equipment, arms, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In addition to that, a secret system of communications is being established, I must say within a primitive framework, but nevertheless some kind of a communications system, as far as I could see on the basis of these documents.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Well, of course we had to have this in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You know, in Bosnia, when we had the first multiparty elections, I had to have three reserve headquarters, because in the first headquarters that I had, in the Holiday Inn hotel in Sarajevo, the first thing that happened was that there was a power breakdown, that there was no water, et cetera, so then I had to have backup systems. That's what the communists taught me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. So then arms were purchased, and channels were sought for that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Well, no, no. Oh, come on, it didn't start already then, as late as that. I mean, let's be fair about this. Let's be honest. We did not start preparing ourselves then. What Sarajevo and Zagreb shared was finance. Not a single people in the former Yugoslavia did not give the kind of contribution that the Croat people gave to their defence and to their freedom. I must say that during the war in Sarajevo, we collected one million deutschemarks during two years of the war, and I know Croats who gave one million marks per person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No, I have to tell you something else. Many people said that I was the best speaker in the HDZ. We attended various rallies, primarily in Germany and western Europe. Since I was a well-known communist dissident, and I was a journalist working for the German radio, and our guest workers abroad listened to that for ten years, and also at that time there were two things only that were reactionary in Zagreb, and that was the football club of Dynamo and the newspaper Vjesnik. I was well-liked amongst these guest workers. First of all, I spoke their language. And they gave a lot of money that went to Zagreb. You see, my political position would not have been that weak had I not lost these financial channels. Finance was in Zagreb. And when this happened, I said, "Gentlemen, it is natural that you buy weapons," and may I say straightaway that they liked this a lot. You know, weapons is the best business of all, anywhere. Let me tell you one more thing so you don't have to ask me afterwards. Since I represented the urban population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was a citizen who could not bring a rifle to his nearest and dearest in Sarajevo. Strategically speaking, at that time, I appointed two men who would be involved in arms supplies and the distribution of arms. That was Mate Boban for Herzegovina and Iko Stanic for Posavina. I must say this was done for practical reasons. These are two different sides, and then there is the border with Croatia, which is very propulsive. And after all, where the Croatian population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are getting some way from the topic now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let us try to sum this up. These efforts to organise the self-defence of the Croat people were taking place at the time when the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have its own legal army, so to speak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Well, until the day of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we did not have a legal army. And I must say that the prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a Croat. So it's not that we didn't want that; we simply did not have an army of our own. Because the Communists gave us the weapons of the Territorial Defence, and the army was the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is precisely what I wish to say: that at that time, the JNA, as the only legal army, so to speak, was already serving the interests of a policy aimed at a Greater Serbia. And the Territorial Defence did not have any weapons, and on the other hand, in terms of organisation, it was set up close to the JNA. That's what you just said now, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Please, until Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state, the Territorial Defence was absolutely an outpost of the JNA, and the JNA leaders left on the 4th of April, 1992. It is only then that we entered the premises of the Territorial Defence, and of course we realised that they were empty, and we started self-organising ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I don't want it to seem as if you and I were only having this discussion. Could you please look at the Honourable Trial Chamber as much as possible while you answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, the finale of what we are talking about right now, all these efforts aimed at the self-defence of the Croat people that took place throughout '91, and in part in 1992, led to the establishment of the Croatian Defence Council on the 8th of April, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I think that that did not have to happen. You see, at the time, we already had the Territorial Defence, and the presidency tried to make a compromise so that all patriotically oriented persons would be included. And we said that all military formations that would be defending Bosnia and Herzegovina should be called the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, the HVO did not agree to be within that, but they agreed to be within the patriotic front of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is precisely what I wanted to ask you right now. As you were then a member of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at one of the meetings that were held in mid-April 1991, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic informed the presidency that the Croatian Defence Council sent on the 10th of April, 1992, that is to say two days after --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Sorry, you're making a mistake. First you said '91, and now you're saying '92, and we're not talking about '91; we're talking about 1992. Both dates are 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: It was a slip of the tongue, I'm sorry. We are talking about '92.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So I'm saying that the HVO, in this letter dated the 10th of April, 1992, submitted a proposal to the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina to establish a joint command for the defence of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina; do you remember that letter?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But if my information is correct, Alija Izetbegovic never put this proposal to the vote; that is, the presidency never managed to pass a formal decision on this.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: You see, that's not the problem, that he did not put this to the vote. But as of that date, there was permanent negotiation between Izetbegovic and Tudjman. As for the collapse of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Milosevic [sic] and Tudjman did not respect the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina because they needed a third Muslim side, and Izetbegovic liked that a lot. And I must say that among others, one of the misfortunes of Bosnia and Herzegovina is that Izetbegovic and Tudjman cannot stand the sight of one another, and as history would have it, I was between the two of them. So unfortunately I did not manage to convince them that joint defence is the only way out. However, in the autumn of 1995, when they finally found a common tongue, and before the Dayton Accords, when we opposed the Serb aggression, the results were fantastic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us not deviate from the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's now 11.00, and we're going to adjourn for our usual break. Do you have very much more to put to this witness? About how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, I must say that I have quite a few questions, and I think that I will at least need the rest of today and perhaps a bit of our time tomorrow as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Kindly confine yourself to the rest of today, which should be more than enough, in my judgement. Mr. Kovacic, do you have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we did not decide definitely; but if we will have, it will be within 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Nice, what's the position about other witnesses this week and this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think there's no problem with this witness for tomorrow. I've not been informed of any. I have another witness arriving today who can start immediately after this witness, I hope, and then, depending on how we seem to be doing, I think there is another witness we may be able to get for later in the weeks as well. So I think we'll have a full -- we should have a full week of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a short week, of course; we're not sitting Friday, remember. It's the holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We should have a full week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. 11.00 -- 11.30, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, a remark, comment from interpreters. Address more to me than to you. They told us we were too fast, especially when -- during our exchanges, and it was particularly French interpreters who objected to that and said that it created difficulties for them. And for Judge Bennouna I would like to apologise for any inconvenience that we have caused. Now, Mr. Kljuic, let us conclude with the topic we were talking about before. That is self-organisation, self-defence and things like that. You will agree with me, I suppose, that the Bosniak Herzegovina HDZ, at the time when you were its President, started organising what we mentioned before, started organising the future army of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those were -- this was the embryo.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I will not agree with your formulation. We were getting ready, but for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina's state, that was my position. Not only for the preparation of Croats, because that concept would mean three -- the armies of three peoples and therefore a conflict. There is no political document. There is no political option which opposes the interests of Croats while being the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: No, no, no. It is not the objectives which are in dispute. I was simply trying to round off the thought, but we already discussed those details and there is no need for me to go back to that. And the second and last thing in this dilemma. We shall agree that all those preparations were done to prepare the defence against the aggression by the so-called JNA, which was formed by paramilitary Serb units and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Exclusively, only against the paramilitary forces of the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, let us move on to another topic. We termed it the co-operation with Muslims, which is what they called themselves then, and I shall ask you now a few questions in this regard. Mr. Kljuic, I suppose you know Mr. Adil Zulfikarpasic quite well, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: He was one of the founding fathers of the Party for Democratic Action at the time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: However, later on he left the SDA and founded or, rather, participated in an organisation which was called the Muslim Bosniak organisation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, did you know that in March 1991 Adil Zulfikarpasic negotiated with Croats in the Republic of Croatia and the Slovenians, and the negotiations bore upon the Proclamation of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the same day as Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No, I did not know that, and it is irrelevant, because there was the European commission that sent us an ultimatum to conduct a referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But we shall talk about this later.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No, no, no. But this is important. We could not proclaim our independence until we were giving the guarantees of the European union that they would recognise us. And they told us, no problem, you will also get it on the basis of the commission's findings, but before that you must conduct a referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is not in dispute, Mr. Kljuic. But it was a year later, I am referring to March 1991.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I do not know the contents of talks conducted by Mr. Adil Zulfikarpasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In the record Z2736 I noted, and that is the minutes of the meeting of the presidency of the HDZ of BiH on the 31st of July '91, that the Bosnia-Herzegovina and HDZ insisted that the Croat people should not disrupt its relations with Muslims. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You even concluded that you had to explain to people on the ground that there was a very broad, larger Serbian campaign conducted with a view to disrupting the relations between the Croats and the Muslims. And yet, on the other hand, you were following what the other side, if I may put it that way, the Muslim people and especially its party, the SDA, was doing at the time.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: But, of course, needless to say, we followed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, as a politician you must have known that in June '91 -- that in June 1991 Alija Izetbegovic proposed to conduct secret negotiations with Serbia on the establishment of a Federation between Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Such information never reached me, but Izetbegovic did conduct various talks with Serbs. I knew that, and, of course, your quotation a few moments ago about Adil Zulfikarpasic. However, lengthy talks with Izetbegovic, it was very important for me to create, in Bosnia at least, a coalition between Croats and Muslims or, rather, Bosniaks today. And they have never stopped explaining that a struggle for independent Bosnia would mean also certain losses, but that it will also mean freedom. On the other hand, continuing within Yugoslavia could have, perhaps, in the early days spared us those losses. But politically, strategically speaking, it would also do away with a Muslim autonomous being. And Milosevic and Karadzic were offering to Izetbegovic to become the second people in Yugoslavia, and I asked them then, "And what is the second people in this Yugoslavia now?" And he answered, "Albanians." So I said, "So, well, they are offering you to be the Albanians?" And, of course, those talks never resulted in any success, even though I am a political adversary of Mr. Izetbegovic today, for reasons into which I do not wish to go into now. But we must pay tribute that he did understand at that time that a struggle for freedom, that the support for the Croat concept was the struggle of the future, and that he refused it to that, because otherwise the outcome of the struggle in the former Yugoslavia would have been quite different had he agreed to that and much more difficult for us Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Right, Mr. Kljuic. But as we are talking about, and Mr. Izetbegovic also confirmed that in one of his speeches that were published. Those talks with the Serbian side, that is those negotiations which were secret up to a point, the Croat public opinion was quite right in suspecting that or, rather, thinking that those negotiations were conducted at the expense of the Croats?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: In the Balkans, any separate talks are always to the detriment of whatever third party. But from the conduct of the Muslim leadership and the citizens, the Croat public, apart from those who wanted to, absolutely had no reason to think that, all the more so, as I have already said it, about 20,000 Muslims went to defend Croatia, and in the parliament and in the government, our views were identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When I said that, I meant the fundamental position of Bosnian Croats who were refusing to remain in whatever shape of Yugoslavia, since that old Yugoslavia was really gone, and for keeps.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Agree. We did not want to stay in any Yugoslavia, let alone rump Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When we're talking about these negotiations of several parties, in an interview once, you said -- I quote you -- "The Croat public needs to understand that I have done at least two things that have secured for me a place in the history of the Croat people. One of them is that I prevented" -- and in quotation marks -- "'a historic agreement' between Karadzic, Filipovic, and Zulfikarpasic." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, first of all, where is it said and when is it said this interview took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) That interview took place sometime in '93, but Mr. Kljuic remembers it. I do not have the text before me. I took it out from somewhere. But Mr. Kljuic now confirms it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Kljuic. It may be, but if counsel is going to quote something at a witness, he should know the place where it comes from, rather than just coming along and quoting it. Now, Mr. Kljuic, do you, in fact, remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, because that was the substance of my philosophy, and I can always repeat it or reproduce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski, what is it you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I want Mr. Kljuic to tell us, what kind of an agreement was that supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: It had to do with the plan Ram, R-a-m. Had Milosevic succeeded in winning over the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then arm them and push them to fight against Croatia, the war would have taken a completely different course. But apart from the political talks that I conducted with Muslim leaders, you should also know that I placed a great trust, both as a citizen and as a pro-Bosnian, that I placed a great trust in the Muslim people. And in the elections of 1990, I won relatively the largest numbers of all the members of the presidency, and the number of those who had voted for me far exceeded the number of Croats with suffrage rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So we can then agree that these agreements that we are talking about were bad for the Croats, for their future destiny?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Well, those agreements were not bad because Milosevic did not succeed. Had Milosevic succeeded in having those negotiations in the way he wanted, they would have been fatal for the Croat people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Right, thank you. On the 27th of August, '91, the presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued instructions to municipal HDZ boards -- and it is document Z13 -- ordering, if I may put it that way, the municipal boards to establish contact with the SDA for the joint preparation of defence?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
