utterances.text: Yes, and it was also applied in practice, namely Croats were sharing with Serbs only four or five municipalities, apart from large towns, and cities, of course. And a countless number of municipalities had Muslims as their neighbours. So what is more natural than to establish an alliance to defend one against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But in this document, it is also said that where the relations between Croats and Muslims are not particularly good, they should be improved at whatever cost, because that would serve the defence.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But let us finish with this document, Z13. This document also envisages a third possibility, if I may put it that way, and that is that if agreed preparations for a defence fail, that then one should organise on one's own?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: And what else could we do, then? There was yet another thing, that disputes in some municipalities should be then settled in Sarajevo, at the highest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Document Z16, and those are the conclusions of the Security Council of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the 18th September, '91, item 5, so that as president you were charged with establishing contact with the SDA presidency, and asking them to tell you what was their political will in that regard, what was their political position in that regard?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And this means that the HDZ had decided to develop a joint action programme with the SDA party for the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: That was what I was aspiring to. I'm not quite sure that all the municipal boards wanted that, but whatever the case, when you are under threat, when you are in a difficult position, then you have to devise a programme which will help you to avoid as many avenues as possible, and Muslims simply were our allies in the defence against Greater Serbian fascism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, do you know Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I do. You mean Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: For a while, you were both members of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I brought him to become the head of the general staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You mean the army, but at first it was the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But do you know that in September '91, Mr. Halilovic had begun organising the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Well, it's a long story about the Patriotic League, you know. I know one thing: that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed by six people, including the late Mustafa Alalovic [phoen], "Italian"; Jerko Doko, Minister of Defence; Stjepan Siber, general; Dragan Vikic, head of the police; and my humble self. And there were some patriotic organisations, paramilitaries, like Green Berets, Patriotic League. But today there is really more talk about it than I knew at the time when I was organising the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina in April '92. It is possible that Mr. Halilovic was amongst those people in the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I agree with you about some things, but I'm not talking about the organisation of the defence at the Bosnian-Herzegovinian level. All I wanted to ask you was what you were to the Patriotic League as the army of the Party of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: It was never formed as the army of the Party for Democratic Action. At that time, a Sarajevo lad called Juka Prazina had more troops than the whole Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let me just mention that Halilovic, in his book, "A Cunning Strategy," described in detail the organisation of the Patriotic League, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Excuse me, but at that time, the establishment of whatever military formations, especially with some religious prefix, meant disorganising Bosnia-Herzegovina from inside. Had they said that it was an SDA army, we wouldn't have been able to set up the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which, in the beginning, had 40 per cent of Croats and Serbs amongst its men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All I wanted to say when I asked you about the Patriotic League -- and this had to do with your attempt that we talked about a while ago, that the HDZ and the SDA should jointly defend Bosnia-Herzegovina -- all I wanted to see and hear from you was that in parallel with those efforts that you are referring to concerning joint defence, this Patriotic League was formed, which was a part of one -- one army or one party.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Right, but most of them had very close relations with Croatia. Most of them had been to the Croatian front, and if you are asking about the supply of weapons, most of it came from Croatia; that is, the only outlet into the world was from Croatia, through coordination with Croatia. Some of the Croatian generals were helping the Patriotic League; that is people who were ready to defend Bosnia. Of course, it was formulated later on and they tried to create the image of a Patriotic League, but those were simply patriots who were trying to help in the defence of their homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, as the then-president of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina and member of the presidency, were you aware that on the 8th of February, 1992, at Mehurici, Halilovic organised a military conquest of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. At that time, I was in a hospital, severely ill, but I didn't know it. I suppose I would have learned that even while in hospital had such an information been available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you wouldn't know anything about those details?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No, I don't, and I must tell you that the Patriotic League as a formation was never -- that nobody knew about it, even when, at that time, when in the form of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we were trying to create the defence front, the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina were to include the Territorial Defence, which was the embryo of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then the HVO, a number of independent groups, and HOS, the HOS. Of all these components, only the HOS agreed to join the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I simply want to tell you that the Patriotic League was never mentioned as a specific and fully-fledged formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but we need to agree that it did exist on the ground.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: On the ground, that they were men who began to claim later on that they were members of the Patriotic League. But as a formation, we knew about the HVO forces, we knew about the HOS, Territorial Defence troops, and we knew about some formations led by some young men who would call themselves this or that. But there was never a formation which would be called the 1st Platoon of the Patriotic League, or anything like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, can we agree that until the threat of war was proclaimed on the 8th of April, 1992, the government and presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina actually did not do anything to organise the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina for defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the witness has been answering that question for quite some time now. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us go on, as instructed by His Honour, to another topic, and this has to do with the support of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina for a sovereign and independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, if we could call it that. You were the president of the HDZ in highly turbulent times when the former common state definitely fell apart?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: As the president of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you personally did not take part in what could be called highly tense and difficult extended talks between the former presidents of all the republics of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I could not participate by the position I held, because there was only one representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that was Alija Izetbegovic. He was primus inter pares. He was president of the presidents of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so he was the only one who took part. But so that we should not be damaged, we authorised Dr. Franjo Tudjman to globally represent our interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I am trying to be as brief as possible, so you already answered another question that I had intended to ask. A quick overview of the international negotiations and the positions taken by the individual peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina regarding the internal set-up of the republic. With the dissolution of Yugoslavia, the question that inevitably arose was what would happen to Bosnia-Herzegovina if it too became an independent and sovereign state, what kind of internal set-up it would have. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The same question was posed before the International Community. So in September, for the sake of chronology, in September 1991 Lord Carrington started with his activities talking to representatives of all three peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina about the future structure of the state?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. With the leaders of all three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You were then expected to provide certain proposals and concepts?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So to cover this ground quickly, can we agree that the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina actually advocated a Bosnia and Herzegovina that would be organised as a confederation of three equal peoples, but with the addition that they felt that that future Bosnia-Herzegovina must remain within the framework of the new Yugoslavia, and if that were to prove impossible, in that case Bosnia-Herzegovina should be divided up.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Milosevic wanted all Serbs to live in one country, and that is a well-known theory of his, and you see after the war the Serbs ended up in the same position as the Germans after the Second World War. As far as the SDS is concerned in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was absolutely against any Bosnia-Herzegovina as a normal state, even though the commission recognised the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be identical to that of other republics. They were gaining time preparing themselves for military action so that actually they offered false proposals, such as a confederation, a tripartite to Bosnia-Herzegovina consisting of three peoples, but from the beginning until the end the aim was always the same, a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Can we go on now to the positions held by another people. The Muslims, you will agree, adopted the position that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be organised as a unitary state based on the principle: One man, one vote?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: They wanted a civil society, but, you know, people who don't understand and don't like Bosnia supported those theses. You see, we had an arrangement, and that was that in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina we should introduce a chamber of peoples with the same number of representatives of all the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in that chamber the representatives of each people would have the right to veto those acts of law which would jeopardise vital national interests. That chamber of peoples is something we have today in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the other hand, regarding the structure of power sharing in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the arrangement was one that we implemented, that at high positions in the Federation, that is in joint political bodies of all three peoples, we should have a parity representation of all three peoples, which means in the presidency there would be two Croats, two Muslims, two Serbs. And at the municipal level that the representation should be proportional. So that would not be an unitary state, but simply the concept unitary, because the Muslim majority was used by those who wanted to carve up Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So I could agree with you in principle regarding the explanation you have given regarding the regulations which would place a minority on an equal footing with the majority, but, apart from those measures, by applying this principle, one man, one vote, the majority people would gain a leading role. That is the gist of the matter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: You are talking in hypotheses. The Serbs were a majority people in the former Yugoslavia and Josip Broz developed a structure through which they were not able to impose that majority at the highest level. It was only when Milosevic toppled the constitutional order that the Serbs managed to gain a majority position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is exactly what we are talking about. We are talking about the structure of the future Bosnia-Herzegovina, not the socialist Bosnia-Herzegovina that was formed as a republic within Yugoslavia as a result of the elections. But this principle of one man, one vote was a principle insisted upon by Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I told you what we sought. With the chamber of peoples and a parity at the top level of authority, all interests would be protected, if it were introduced. Yes, but you see we had the right to decision-making in those talks because any change, any change of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina required a two-thirds majority. Therefore, there wasn't a single bill that could inaugurate an unitarian state. And one man, one vote is a natural law in all European states, including multi-national ones such as Switzerland or Belgium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, are you going to move onto another topic now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to round off this topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But let me summarise what you have just said in answer to the previous question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no need, Mr. Naumovski, to summarise what the witness has said. We have his answers and that is sufficient. Now, unless there is something new to ask about this topic, I suggest that we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: My final question on this topic. Can we agree, Mr. Kljuic, that Bosnia and Herzegovina, when it became independent at the referendum, was faced with the unsolved problem of its future organisation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: It is normal, when a country is moving from a socialist into a democratic system, and furthermore, when it is pulling out other common homeland, that it should not have a fully formulated political structure. But if there had been peace and if democratic talks could have been possible, there is no doubt that Bosnia-Herzegovina would have reached a compromise, as is the case in many countries going through such a transition. Only those who question the independence and identity of Bosnia-Herzegovina, calling it a Communist creation, an unreasonable state, an irrational entity, wanted it to break up. Bosnia-Herzegovina is an old state with thousand a years behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I agree with you, absolutely, that solutions would have been found. But immediately after the Proclamation of independence, a month later the aggression occurred, a war broke out because one people tried by force to impose its policies. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. All that is true. Before that there was the aggression against Slovenia, then the aggression against Croatia, and at that point in time, when the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina occurred, a third of the state of Croatia was occupied. And yet it did not give up its intention to create a state. So that was not a reason, if Serb paramilitaries and the JNA attacked Bosnia-Herzegovina, we won't give up the idea of Bosnia-Herzegovina just like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Naumovski --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I want to know, where is this supposed to be assisting the Trial Chamber? We have been through, at some length, these constitutional questions. The witness gave very specific evidence about his role in these matters. Now, where are you heading with these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if Your Honours consider these questions to have been clearly presented, I will go on. But we consider these to be very important issues, as this is a period covered by our indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've been going over the same topics for some time. Now, what is the next topic you are going to speak of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just going to reach that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you mind --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, what is the topic, Mr. Naumovski, that you are going to move to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the topic I am about to embark upon are the positions of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina from which we see its support for a sovereign and independent Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Embark upon it as quickly as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do so promptly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So let us focus on this topic now, Mr. Kljuic. We have already agreed that from the very beginnings of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you personally advocated the sovereignty and independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In one of the first documents regarding military threats, Z2725 of the 25th of January '91, you expressed your position that you were against threats to the sovereignty, freedom and territorial integrity of any republic in the interests of any people.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. But it was stated then that if Croatia were to be attacked we would defend it. That was the day before a falsified film was to be shown about Spegeli. It was aired three times in Sarajevo and 24 times in 24 hours in Belgrade, because the idea was to create an atmosphere in which a Serbhood was being in jeopardy, and this had a very strong propaganda effect, this film.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You spoke in the transcript in 2546, 2542, in the transcript, but let me not repeat. The weapons procured by the Republic of Croatia was exclusively for defence against aggression, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We've already spoken about the activities of the SDS parties and the plans of the Serbs, but perhaps it is important to note that on the 26th of April '91 the first community of municipalities was formed called the Community of Municipalities of Bosnian Krajina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In document Z2733, and those are the minutes of the HDZ presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 16th of April 1991, you extended full support to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the preservation of the territory integrity of the republic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. The Prime Minister was Mr. Jure Pelivan, a member of the HDZ, and it was only normal to prevent the formation of these SAO's, which were an introduction to the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The SAO being autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And by that same document you condemn any redrawing of borders?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, during your examination-in-chief mention was made, when talking about the positions within the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina regarding the future set-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina, mention was made of a meeting held on the 13th of June 1991 in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you attended that meeting, a few questions about it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In order to understand the time frame when the meeting was held, let me remind you of a few events that occurred just prior to the 13th of June 1991. The meeting was held just after the events at the Plitvice lakes in the Republic of Croatia when the Serbs took over the police station?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That was the first armed conflict of paramilitary forces and the Croatian police in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that that was the first one. For me, the first occurred on -- between the 17th and 18th of August in 1990, when the barricades were put up in Knin and when helicopters of the Croatian police tried to head towards Knin and they were intercepted by airplanes of the Yugoslav Air Force. But it is quite certain that after that event came the incident in Plitvice, followed by the incident in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I was just going to say that in Borovo Selo, Serb paramilitary forces [indiscernible] 12 Croats, and this meeting was held when the so-called SAO Krajina took a decision on separation from the Republic of Croatia and annexation to the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And only a day after Presidents Tudjman, Izetbegovic and Milosevic had held a meeting in Split?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. In the villa Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And again, chronologically, a day after President Izebegovic gave instructions for secret talks with the Serbs that we referred to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So let me shorten all of this. So this meeting was held at a time when the war in Croatia hadn't really begun, but it was quite clear that it was about to break out?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: You forgot to mention another detail. If there had been any doubt up to now that a meeting had been held in Karadjordjevo, after Hrvoje Sarinic's book with photographs and the first written document on the 26th of March 1991, the meeting in Karadjordjevo was held, so you must place that meeting within the overall context of the situation such as it was on the 13th of June. We wanted to quote a series of meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but you must admit that this was one of capital significance?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We just wanted to mention these as background material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So not only was the war inevitable, but the dissolution of Yugoslavia was also inevitable by then, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I assume what you are trying to convince me of. But let me give you a very simple answer. All these things were insignificant if we accept international law and the Helsinki conference. Iraq captured Kuwait and the government went into exile, but it was a legal government in exile. All these elements, all these events that occurred before the 13th of June, did not give us any right not to believe in the future of a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina and a sovereign Croatia. I must tell you that at that meeting, there was such statements and such individuals who were speaking as if they were in a marketplace, as if all this was over. And one of them was saying, "Add those two municipalities, Jablanica and Konjic, to me," and I said, "But that's not possible; those are the only two municipalities where the SDA won the elections, and they have 70 per cent of the population." And he answered, "But I need them for the sake of communications." So you see, I can accept that the background, the context, was very difficult, and that it was very difficult for an ordinary citizen to find his way and to understand all this. But the people who were leading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I think we've got this point. Mr. Naumovski, is there anything else you want to ask about this topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes. In connection with this, what I wanted, Your Honour, was to discuss with Mr. Kljuic what it was that he proposed at that meeting, and not other people, if I may be allowed to put several questions in that connection to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put to the witness -- or rather ask the witness what he proposed, and then perhaps, if he could answer shortly, we can get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, from the minutes Z2717, minutes of the meeting held on the 27th of December, '91 -- you have it before you. This is this thick document -- on page 24/1, allow me to read it to you. You certainly remember what you said, and you said that at the meeting on the 13th of June '91, three options had been presented regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina which the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina advocated in view of the circumstances that prevail at a given moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What page is this in the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) 63, Your Honours, in the English text. In the Croatian version, 24/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The first option was to struggle for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as that is possible. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, of course, that is authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And second, if the Serbs take their own, go into a confederation with the Republic of Croatia and the rump Bosnia-Herzegovina with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Third, if the Serbs won their own and the Muslims do not wish to go into a confederation with the Republic of Croatia, then a part of the Muslims needs to be won over and the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the majority Croatian population be annexed to the Republic of Croatia. If I understand the minutes well, the ideas were yours, and they were elaborated by Mr. Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No, no. There were three options, depending on the outcome of the dissolution of Yugoslavia. This was said on the 13th of June, and it was only quoted here. Of course, if there is no Bosnia-Herzegovina, if the Muslims wish to have some kind of confederation with us, that was the natural way towards the West, and if no one wants to go with you, what is more natural than to remain on your own? But those are hypotheses which I did not work on, nor did I say that the third option should be adopted as the first, and that is the difference between those others and me, because I lay down the theory as to what things could look like given certain circumstances. But at the meeting already on the 13th of June -- that is, six and a half months prior to this -- many had already started working towards the third option and against the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was the reason for vast losses for our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But let me just remind Your Honours that Mr. Kljuic spoke about these things also in the interview published in the Rijeka Novi List, which has today been admitted into evidence. I must object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Mr. Naumovski, for the moment, you are examining the witness, and the purpose is, as expeditiously as possible, to ask the questions which are relevant as far as this trial is concerned. Now, you've been examining him for nearly two hours, and there must come a limit to the amount of time which is available and which the Court can allow for this examination. Now, we have these minutes of the meeting. Unless there is something else that you want to ask arising from them, I suggest that we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I think that Mr. Kljuic just answered and agreed --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No, no, no. This detail about the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to continue this argument. Now, would you move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us move along chronologically.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: A year later, in 1992, the co-chairmen of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen, presented five possible approaches to resolving the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I talked to Lord Owen and to Mr. Cyrus Vance, but the only point of the Vance-Owen Plan that was accessible to me was the one that divided Bosnia-Herzegovina into ten plans [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This happened later, these five possible approaches. I imagine that you, as president of the HDZ and a member of the presidency of the republic, were aware of this. The first possibility was to organise Bosnia-Herzegovina as a centralised state?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, we are going to proceed, in line with what we've been told by the honourable Judges. The presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 10th of July 1992, the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina say that they do not want to remain in rump Yugoslavia. We've already taken care of that, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: As a result of the increasingly difficult situation in the former Yugoslavia, Bosnia-Herzegovina included, the 6th of August, 1991, in Prozor, a meeting was held of the main board of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us just remind the Court that the main board is actually the highest body within the HDZ between two congresses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This document, document Z10, shows that for the umpteenth time, the sovereignty and indivisibility of Bosnia-Herzegovina was supported?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Point 19, paragraph 1, says that the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina remains on its previous position that we just quoted, but will never allow the Croatian people to be treated as a national minority, nor will it allow other peoples to seek agreement on the fate of Bosnia and Herzegovina without the participation of the Croats?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The conclusions, Mr. Kljuic, from this meeting that Z10 refers to -- that is, this meeting that was held on the 6th of August of 1991 -- are the platform of the HDZ and these newly created conditions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, you can put it that way, although our platform did not undergo any changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I know, I know. I just wanted to say that the conditions had changed within one year's time.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, the conditions changed, but the policy did not. You are saying here that they would not accept outvoting, Croats would not accept it, and that they will not agree that somebody else discusses Bosnia without them. But these things go back to 1990 and the documents adopted then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So we've agreed on that, and let's move on.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In spite of all these events that we have just presented to the Honourable Trial Chamber, in this document, you insist on independence and indivisibility; but in Point 22 of document Z10, you add that in case a war breaks out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, through the attack of a Greater Serb or any other aggressor against the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a special plan will be resorted to; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. The special plan was not supposed to destroy the constitutional setup of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If there is an attack from any side, then there is a plan in terms of self-organisation, links, supplies, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is precisely what point 19 says, that the Croat people would self-organise themselves?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us skip part of this chronology, but at any rate, chronologically speaking, the war has already broken out in Croatia; the first air attack took place against Zagreb; Dubrovnik was shelled; I just want to refresh your memory in terms of the period that we're interested in right now. Basically this was a very difficult time for the Croatian people in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right? Please, could you just give an audible answer for the sake of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and I must say that at that time we expressed great solidarity, and we sent a convoy of aid to the people of Dubrovnik. We sent a lot of people to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Through these elements that I try to present as briefly as possible now, I even skipped a few, could we say that this is a time when the world started showing an interest in Yugoslavia? The U.S.A. still adhere to the position that Yugoslavia had to remain as such?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The statement made by Secretary of State Baker was disastrous for us. Zimmermann had a different opinion, but the international community, from the very outset, was quite indifferent toward Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This is precisely what leads me to the question that that is why it was politically wise to bear in mind all the implications of everything that was going on, and also to have solutions envisaged for all possible situations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Please, I have to tell you once again, it is different if we are brought into a position to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is another thing altogether if some people from the HDZ and from the highest quarters in the HDZ wanted to take part in this and actually did. That is to say we did have certain points in our programme, but first we had to advocate the first, and then -- for as long as possible, and everything else worked in our favour. They guaranteed our first point, and that is to say the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The fact that some people did not want to recognise international law and to hear what was going on, to their regret and to the misfortune of all of us, they did not do this, and the Croat people were simply divided in half.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. Kljuic, that's what I wish to clarify with you right now. On the 8th of October, 1991, a meeting was held of the presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the republican crisis staff of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is document Z18. And you chaired that meeting. In point 4 of the minutes, it says, "The HDZ will continue to advocate an independent, indivisible Bosnia-Herzegovina if possible." Z18, if you need it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: It's not necessary. I know that I always said that we would advocate Bosnia-Herzegovina until the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But now it continues, if Bosnia-Herzegovina were to be broken up, then the top people of the Muslim population, if there is a secession of the so-called Serb territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslims, together with Croats, should remain together within a single territory, and they should reach a confederacy, and our territories could perhaps be linked by way of a contract to Croatia and Slovenia, respectively?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, all of that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right. So we don't have to repeat all that. That is what you repeated to your interview in the Rijeka Novi List on the 13th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Oh, yes, but then there is one thing that is wrong in Novi List, and that is where it says that division is the only way out. Although I denied this, they did not accept it, and also the Muslim nationalists until the present day in their books say that -- they quote this as an example that I was in favour of a division. Please find a single document where I am in favour of partition except in this falsified document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, when you get to a convenient moment, we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I know, Your Honour, that you asked for an adjournment as early as possible, and I agree that we can do it right now, if it's convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now and sit again at half past 2.00. Mr. Kljuic, if you would be back again then, please, half past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.40 p.m. 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Before I begin, I should merely like to say, and something that is also good news for Mr. Kljuic, that during the break I considered the view of Your Honours regarding the facts deemed relevant by the Court, and I have completely restructured my cross-examination, which I had planned for this afternoon. Which means I shall need a lot less time than I thought I would, than I told you this morning when asked about it by Your Lordship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, before we do anything, there seems to be something wrong with my receiver here. Mr. Naumovski, we'll go on. I can follow on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, as I have promised the Court, and you will find it easier, I've cut my questions short, and the Court has already heard on various matters, so there is no need to go back to that. Before the lunch break we were talking about different options, including a confederative association. We shall agree that on the 18th of March 1994, the so-called preliminary accord was signed in Washington on the federation between, on the one hand the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Republic of Croatia on the other.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. One of the clauses of the Washington Accords was a possibility for confederation and federation with the Republic of Croatia, but to simplify matters it would mean petitioning of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because even if the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina becomes a confederation with the Republic of Croatia, then what else can the Serb side do but join Yugoslavia? So that this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kljuic, could you please try to slow down. As of the beginning I tried to follow you in English, in French, unfortunately not in Serbo-Croatian because I don't really understand that language well. The interpreters simply are having a very difficult time following you. It is a speed which we simply cannot keep us with. So will you please try to keep a check on the speed of your speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. I shall do my best. So the Washington Accords, and there were a number of decisions incorporated in it, including Mate Boban withdrawal from political life. So the document also envisaged the end of a war between the Muslims and the Croats, then the setting up of a federation which would serve as a basis for the definitive liberation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, among other things, a possibility was announced of setting up a confederation between the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. However, in Bosnia-Herzegovina nobody ever, and at that time we still had the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and after Washington all the HDZ representatives also took part in sessions. Nobody ever confirmed this particular form of Federation. Quiet to the contrary, it was rejected in very clear terms. We know that the political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina was resolved at a later stage through the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All I wanted was to get a clear picture about numerous options which were on the table both from abroad, from foreign sides, and from the inside, from the territory itself. And they were all laid on the table.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, it is quite true that the confederal option was one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. I had prepared several questions covered by the topic of regionalisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But of all those documents that make part of the file, a document, Z2744, is perhaps the most precise. That is an excerpt from the minutes of a session of the presidency of BiH HDZ, of the 26th of August '91, when it was decided to accept the proposal on the regionalisation of municipal boards of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And that was done so as to improve the structure of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina and also to improve the work of the HDZ subordination?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Subordination. If I may, neither the presidency nor I as the President could not maintain daily contact with 79 municipal organisations. So that we set up four or five regional organisations. And they would come to Sarajevo, receive their instructions, and then would disseminate them and distribute them on the ground. It had no political implications at all. It's said to do with the party organisation only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but it was to improve your functioning, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, today we went in great -- into great detail when we tried to portray the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina at a moment of disintegration of the former Yugoslavia and at a time when the new Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had not become independent yet. So I am referring to the latter half of 1991 and the first two months of '92. We've agreed, I believe, and you just repeated it a while ago, that there were all sorts of political opinions, both within and without the HDZ, as to the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We are agreed that we already covered those topics?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And all those theses were basically discussed before the Muslims and Croats at a referendum held on the 22nd of February and the 1st of March '92, voted for the independence and sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are sorry, we could not hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Although many options were considered, the political programme, the only political programme was a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was another matter when we talked about option A, B, C, or whatever, but we never said, "Right, as of today, we don't want a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina any more." Quite the reverse: When it was confirmed by the referendum, then any behaviour that would run counter to that would go against the interests of the Croat people in the first place, and ultimately would also be against the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But lamentably, it was only the Muslims and the Croats who were deciding on the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because the Serbs were emphatically against the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No, that is not so, my dear sir. You can look up the results of the referendum, and you will see that every third Serb in Bosnia-Herzegovina voted "For" in the referendum, although in many municipalities the SDS terrorised the population and would not let people go out and vote. Namely -- I have to clarify certain matters here. The census showed that Muslims accounted for 44 per cent of the population, but as they have many children, they were only 39 per cent on the voters' list, on the voters' rosters. Croats, with their population belonging in an older age group in Bosnia-Herzegovina, even though they accounted for 17,3, according to the census, yet they accounted for about 20 or 21 per cent of the voters' rosters. If all the Muslims and Croats -- not all the Muslims and not all the Croats voted, for various technical reasons, then it is out of the 64 or 65 per cent, which was the turnout at the referendum for independence, a considerable percentage -- that is, of about 8 or 9 per cent -- were the Serbs who had turned out and voted, since the Serbs accounted for 31 per cent of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It becomes a very important political fact that every third Serb was for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Right. I will accept your reprimand. I generalised something which I shouldn't have; I meant the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Quite, but their political attitude after the political referendum was even more -- obviously more conspicuous, more glaringly against an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And we agreed that that attitude of theirs then ended in a war shortly after the proclamation of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, one could put it that way, but I prefer to say that that war was being prepared for quite some time, and that it was being prepared in Belgrade, and that the SDS leadership and Bosnian Serbs would have never been able to do all that evil that they did in Bosnia had they not enjoyed the logistics, direct military help, and all the indirect assistance coming from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kljuic, let us address another topic. Today you mentioned the political platform adopted at the HDZ convention on the 25th of March, 1991, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I forgot to show you a document, so will you please look at it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) My I please adduce this document? This is the political platform of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted by the Mostar convention. Will the usher please help us?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I should like to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That is why we are doing this, so that you can have a look.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D97/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, we have a slight technical problem. We have this document, but there is a seal lacking. There is nothing here. It was copied, and then it was sent to various municipal boards.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: The only question is, dear sir, whether this material was distributed before the convention, as a working paper, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: No, look at this. 25th March, '91. Will you please look at it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could, please, the counsel and the witness try not to speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, you're being asked not to speak at the same time as the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I apologise, and now is the umpteenth time that I have to apologise both to the interpreters and to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: This is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We knew nothing about it, and all I wanted from you was to corroborate its authenticity. That is all.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No problem at all. It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kljuic, one question about the nationality -- dual nationality, dual citizenship. In this case we already heard some opinions, and the only thing I wanted to ask you about it is as follows: In the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation signed by presidents Tudjman and Izetbegovic on the 21st of July, 1992, Item 7 says that both the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia will allow their nationals to acquire dual nationality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: And who could the citizens of Muslim origin, citizens -- I mean nationals of Bosnia-Herzegovina who are Muslims, which dual nationality would they have? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I just quoted to you this item. As a member of the presidency, you must be conversant with the document?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: It was signed by the president of the presidency of which you were a member?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So my only question is: Do we agree that this possibility was envisaged by this document?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: The possibility of a dual nationality is not so outlandish, but its interpretation and subsequent use became outlandish, and it is to the detriment and the expense of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Namely, the positive aspect of this dual nationality is that they can travel while holding the passport only and do not need any visas. But it becomes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. There's an objection. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution feels a bit disadvantaged. We do not have the document. I don't know if the Court has it either, and if a copy were available. We would deeply appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You refer to the document of the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have just been reminded that I forgot to produce it. I apologise. I apologise. Unfortunately, we only have it in English, but --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: It is not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This is an Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation of the 21st of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D98/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Naumovski, we have the document of the 25th of March '91, which in English says, "Political Platform of the HDZ-BH," so this is the political platform or the political programme of the HDZ; that is, the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I should like to ask Mr. Kljuic, with regard to that document, what does he think of the first sentence of that document, which says, [In English] "Part of the unified HDZ in the same manner," and so on, [Interpretation] because it does not quite agree with what he told us in the beginning. Does he recognise this position as the position of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as an integral part of the integral HDZ?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: You have to understand this in very specific terms. People from Zagreb brought a tremendous pressure to bear on the convention, and that was the first time that they tried to topple me as the president, and they brought Mate Boban to oppose me. But when they counted the votes, before that, they realised that Boban could not get more than 53 votes of 288. And that was the share of the Herzegovinian and Croats over the Bosnian and Herzegovinian Croats; that is 17 per cent. On the other hand, we did recognise, you know, this unity, you know, there are association, there is an association of social democratic parties or association of conservative parties in Europe, you have the European democratic union which brings together Christian Democratic parties and Conservatives or Liberals, so why couldn't we say that at this particular moment, we in Zagreb are, on the 25th of March, 1991, that we are together? But this document, without the seal and signature, cannot in any way impair the identity, the authenticity of our registration with the Court and the overall political activity of the HDZ. Please, we did not quarrel, we were together. But, under the then laws we had to register, they -- Zagreb, and we had to do it in Sarajevo. So this is now trying to bring back this old thesis, which I wanted to support through the back door. But this was merely of a formal nature because after the convention this document was sent out to the ground and it was more because of those other details, including one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kljuic, Mr. Kljuic. You are telling us that this document was adopted under the Zagreb pressure, under pressure from Zagreb; is that so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No, but the formulation that we are one, that we are integrated. At that moment, to all intents and purposes, we had common interest. But there was no administrative unification. That was not carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, perhaps we could assist Their Honours if we were to repeat something. In those days Yugoslavia still existed and both Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia are republics within one state?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. You must understand, we couldn't separate our defensive intentions from Zagreb. I said a moment ago that Zagreb took our money and also it took upon itself the duty to arm us, because, after all, they had open borders. We in Bosnia had no borders, and nor did we have any possibility of making contact with others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can we proceed, Mr. Kljuic. I have left out a whole set of questions in line with the suggestions of their honours. But maybe just a few more points towards the end of this cross-examination. Mr. Kljuic, in October 1993 you again joined the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I didn't join it again. Because I was eliminated, contrary to the provisions of the constitution. What happened was that conditions were established whereby I could avail myself of my legal position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, but talking about that, did anyone else among the presidency members get replaced in an illegal manner?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No. No one, because not one of them was about to become President of the state. But there were people who walked out of the presidency for political reasons. The first to walk out were Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic. After that Franjo Boras left Sarajevo because he fled to a place of security. And then, at the end, after '93, Fikret Abdic again left, again to a safer place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let me ask you then differently. Were there any illegal appointments?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Oh, yes, indeed. First of all, the person who was brought to take over from me, by agreement between Tudjman, Boban and Izetbegovic, was called Miro Lasic. He had no legal prerequisites to become a member of the presidency, because he had not taken part in the elections. He was not a candidate. And, as you know, the results of the elections produced a list of people by order of the number of votes they got. In the case of death, or any other reason of absence or resignation, instead of that person, the next person on the rating list would join the presidency. However, Izetbegovic, Boban and Tudjman agreed that I should be replaced by Lasic, who was not on that list, nor was he a candidate at the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Were there other persons who joined the presidency?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Similarly, there were persons among the Serbs, when they joined the aggressor ranks. So in a legal manner you have to make a distinction here between the Lasic case, which was anti-constitutional, and the replacement of Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic, who were replaced, as they should be, by the third and fourth persons on the rating list according to the number of votes they received at the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mrs. Tatjana Ljujic Mijatovic, was she a candidate at the elections?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No, she was not. Let me try and explain that for you. After Kecmanovic had left, not a single Serb on the electorial list was on our side, but they changed sides. They switched to the aggressor side. So our legal counsel decided that it would be possible to fill in the vacancy from among parliament members. So Mrs. Ljujic came, who was only a member of parliament in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. But let us continue where we left off. This was just a note in passing. I really wanted to ask you about your resumption of your position in the presidency. Together with you, in October '93, Mr. Ivica Komsic, who is a Croat, and Mr. Nijaz Durakovic joined the presidency at the same time as you, the latter being a Muslim? I don't know whether your "yes" has gone down in the record.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was quite normal and constitutional, because both of them had been candidates at the elections. Ivica Komsic was the third on the Croatian list and Durakovic was the number three on the Muslim list. So it was quite normal that the two of them, when Boras and Abdic had left the presidency, the latter started acting destructively in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was normal to fill in the vacancies in the presidency. That was one of the reasons why I agreed to become active again as a presidency member. I had to overcome the fact that I had been a victim and to swallow my pride, because that was the first time that the presidency acquired the characteristics of a patriotic institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Just one more point. Both Mr. Komsic and Mr. Durakovic, in your opinion, are honourable and decent people who you welcomed and supported their joining the presidency?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, they legitimately joined the presidency, and I was glad that it was Durakovic and Komsic that had joined instead of Boras -- Boras and Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, we should like to show a videotape which is about seven minutes long. And on this clip, which we would like to show you. It was produced by the publishing house, Oslobodenje, based in Sarajevo. I think that the project, the whole project is entitled "Fama."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it relating to, Mr. Naumovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this video clip these three gentlemen that we have just named are speaking. They are members of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina who joined the presidency in October 1993. So he we will hear Mr. Kljuic, briefly, Mr. Komsic and Mr. Durakovic. And I only have one question on that clip for Mr. Kljuic, after we see it. I think it is important. I would like the technical booth to show us this video, but let us first, with the help of the usher, provide Your Honours with a transcript, even though there is an English translation on the video. Croatian for us, so it will be easy for us to understand. It's subtitled in English. Would the technical booth please show us this video, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Videotape will be number D99/1 and the transcript D99A/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, an observation by the Prosecution is it -- this clip appears to have been edited in a number of places, at least two that I was able to observe. And I am not clear that the entire tape is what is there. So I have no way, unfortunately, of knowing for sure. But from our perspective, it appears to be an edited edition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, can you give the original to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said, Your Honours, Mr. Kljuic is here and he can confirm. This was filmed in 1996 by a service or, rather, a company called Oslobodenje. This is the abstract we received indicating Oslobodenje as the author and they filmed 18. We got this video clip which was not edited. It was given to us as an original tape. But Mr. Kljuic is here to confirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you handed over to the Prosecutor all that you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have prepared what we have shown Your Honours for the Prosecution. We have a copy for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there anything else that you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we only have this. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, you can hand it over to the Prosecution afterwards. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you are the most competent person to tell us when this recording was made, to confirm its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: As in September '96 the term of office of the presidency was about to expire, this was recorded as documentation. All I can say is that these are extracts from a lengthier statement and that the quotation is quite authentic, but it is taken out of context, because there was a longer statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But obviously the authors are Oslobodenje?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Well, it's a private company now, you see, so this was done by professionals, by directors and film makers. The source is not in dispute, but I have to say, to be quite frank, that this was taken from a longer interview which was meant to be some kind of a historical testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, just one final question about what we have just seen. Do you agree with what Mr. Komsic and Mr. Durakovic said?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: You see, I didn't know that Komsic went to see Dr. Tudjman, because obviously he wanted some support. I'm quite a different sort of person. I decided to rejoin because my country was going through the most difficult times. And the second reason, this is something that was my right as a result of the elections. And third, though I did not decide on military issues, I did a great deal in the area of human rights protection at the level of the central authorities, and I have to say that I take pride in that, and that this was indeed the only area where it was possible to survive during the war. Of course, I'm talking about politicians with different views, representing different peoples, and so on. However, here, in spite of the most difficult conditions, the right to life was preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Kljuic, I think it is my one-but-last question, but with a bit of reservation, let me show you a diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) With the usher's assistance, I should like to distribute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We will show it to you. It's in English, but you speak English, so you will be able to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is number D100/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours and Mr. Kljuic, this diagram, in black, under the heading "President," we have mentioned the presidents of the HDZ from the period of 1990 until 1992, people who were elected at party conventions. And in red we have marked the so-called acting presidents in the periods in between two congresses. Mr. Kljuic, I have only one question in this connection. I assume you understand this diagram. Do you agree with me that apart from Davor Perinovic, who was president for a very brief period of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, both you and Miljenko Brkic and Mate Boban were elected in an identical fashion: first as acting presidents of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and secondly at a convention or assembly meeting of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you, for the simple reason that all those that followed me took over in wartime, when these regional conventions of theirs cannot be identified with the congress of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What does that mean? What kind of a convention was it in Medjugorje if I, as president, was not invited, if a number of other functionaries representing the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina were not present, such as the prime minister, members of parliament, ministers? A second point I should like to make: It's not the same to replace Davor Perinovic, who was a political fool infiltrated by the Yugoslav KOS or intelligence service with the aim of taking the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina into the war in 1990, and replacing a president who had won in the elections at a convention in peacetime in the presence of all relevant factors of the political life of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, this follows from the documents that have been entered into the record, the documents of the presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Acting presidents, you were an acting president, then Miljenko Brkic, then Mate Boban, in an identical manner. That is what I wanted to say, not the circumstances under which each of these individuals were elected.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: No, but please, slowly. Let us make things quite clear. There can be no convention in Bosnia-Herzegovina which Boban could have won in competition with me, because the support that I enjoyed was incomparable with that that he enjoyed. I was declared by the media to be undesirable. Furthermore, I wish to tell you that had I been invited to the convention, I would certainly have gone to Medjugorje, though I didn't leave Sarajevo until 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Naumovski, I think that after all, we must try and focus the testimony to matters concerning Mr. Kordic and Mr. Cerkez. It is not Mr. Kljuic that is at stake. Let him testify about the situation, but it is not his own position or the conditions under which he came or what he represents that is of direct interest to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, I understand, Your Honours. To be quite frank, we, too, have our own opinion, when a witness is brought like Mr. Kljuic, who is simply a politician who is brought to testify in a criminal case. But I have good news for Your Honours: one more question. So I beg you for your patience just for a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, my final question for you. In the course of July, you were here for a full day answering questions from the Prosecution. Today it was me who questioned you for almost a whole working day. All your answers, the situation that we discussed, was essentially a political presentation of events in the territory of the former Yugoslavia at the time of its disintegration, essentially the political options that were in circulation both on the international stage and within Bosnia-Herzegovina. So we have been discussing political circumstances and the implications of everything that occurred?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, true. What else could you expect to get from me? I was not a witness of any acts. I was not in command. I said in my first sentence -- may I say this: I do not know Mr. Cerkez. I may have seen him two or three times at a rally, but we never had any relationship. I said that what you are charging Mr. Kordic with, I am not a witness for that. We were separate during the war. We didn't see one another for years. The fact that I was his president and that I appointed him to a certain working place and the minor differences we had are quite irrelevant for this trial. Therefore I'm here more in the capacity of an expert, to explain to you that the HDZ had the strongest political line in terms of the maintenance of the sovereignty of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that had people implemented those policies, among other things, there wouldn't have been so many casualties, and they wouldn't be in The Hague. But unfortunately, we do not have sitting here the people who imposed those policies and who imposed an enormous tragedy upon the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, that brings to an end my examination. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And I also thank Your Honours for your patience. Thank you all, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you can finish, I take it, this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I'm sure of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good day to you, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Good day to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My name is Goran Mikulicic. I'm an attorney at law from Zagreb, and together with my colleague Bozidar Kovacic, attorney at law from Rijeka, I represent the interests of Mr. Cerkez. I shall be considerably shorter than my colleague Mr. Naumovski, and I'm going to put eight questions to you, judging by my notes.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, as the leading politician in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and as a member of the supreme state authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina during a critical period in time, can you answer the following question for me: Is it true that from mid-1992 until the end of 1993 -- that is the time period covered by the indictment -- in view of the objective situation, there were ongoing contacts between politicians from the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina respectively at top level? I'm referring to presidents, and, of course, other levels as well. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Kljuic, that during this same period of time, there were also diplomatic relations between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia without any interruption at the level of embassies? That is to say, Bosnia had its embassy in Zagreb and Croatia had its embassy in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Kljuic, that in the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb, there was a logistics centre of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a military/economic representative office, which also had its subsidiary office in Split, throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the military, but I know that there was a logistics centre in Split and in Zagreb. Of course, the ambassador at that time was Mrs. Turkovic, and she was certainly the one in charge of this coordination. You cannot ask me now to answer that, because I was not in Split or in Zagreb at the time, so I cannot really give an answer to that. I didn't see exactly what was going on, but obviously the embassy and the ambassador were quite legal and legitimate and involved in activities that the Croat government was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to give Document D32/2 to Mr. Kljuic in order to refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is the document that I referred to, Mr. Kljuic, when I asked you if you were aware of the fact that in Zagreb, attached to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was a military/economic representative office as well. Can you perhaps recall that detail now? If not, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I said that I did not know about their structure. As for names, I know that Dzevad Topic was there, but it was only a few days that he was there in Zagreb, or a month, and then he went to America. I don't know these people. I know Hasan Cengic, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: These are the persons from this list; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. I should like to thank the usher, and let's move further on. Mr. Kljuic, since you were a member of the supreme government authority in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you know that the state authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina ever adopted a regulation or a law which led to the confiscation of the property owned by private or physical persons from the Republic of Croatia on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was such a confiscation ever carried out? That is to say, were bank accounts frozen, were assets or properties frozen?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about banks because they did not function at the time. And as for immovable property, it was only natural, for war purposes, this was done. Unfortunately, we were handicapped, because we had the least quantity of assets from other republics in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. I know, you're talking about the mobilisation of automobiles, certain properties, buildings, et cetera, for the mobilisation and defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
